lines.cap: **Narrator:** Wednesday. School hall. Emergency: the canteen committee is considering replacing curry puffs with plain rice cakes.
**Mei:** I've entered the **Public Speaking Competition**. I wrote six pages! Listen:
**Mei:** Hello, my name is Mei, and today I am going to talk to you about snacks...
**Mr H:** You have lost the judges in four seconds, and you are hiding behind A4 paper.
**Ethos:** Hold the lectern! Did someone call for **rhetoric** — the ancient art of persuasion?
**Pathos:** We're **Aristotle's Triad**! Formed in Greece, **4th century BC**, still topping the charts!
**Logos:** Statistically, eighty-seven per cent of crowds fall asleep during 'today I am going to talk about'.
**Will:** Why does a Greek boy band get a spotlight?! My soliloquies get fluorescent tubes!
**Mei:** Current speech: **one star**. Curry puff survival odds: grim.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode six: Friends, Romans, Year 8.

chapters.title: Writing for the ear & Aristotle's triad

lines.cap: **Mr H:** Rule one: a speech is written for the **ear**, not the eye. Listeners hear each sentence **once**, at your speed.
**Nib:** Pin down **GAP** before you write: **Genre**, **Audience**, and **Purpose** — to persuade, inform, inspire, or commemorate.
**Mr H:** So mix **short punchy sentences** with longer ones, repeat key ideas, and address the room as '**you**' and '**we**'.
**Ethos:** Now meet the **rhetorical triangle**! I am **Ethos**: character and **credibility**. Why should the audience trust *you*?
**Ethos:** Build ethos through experience, fairness, and honesty — like **Malala Yousafzai** arguing at the UN that 'one book and one pen' can change the world.
**Pathos:** I am **Pathos**: **emotion**! Pity, pride, outrage, hope — stirred through **emotive language** and vivid personal stories!
**Logos:** And I am **Logos**: **logic** and **evidence**! Facts, statistics, clear examples, and step-by-step cause and effect.
**Nib:** Held together by **Kairos**: choosing the right words for the **right moment** and occasion.
**Mei:** Wait — isn't rhetoric just a posh word for lying and manipulating people?
**Mr H:** No. The tools are neutral. Blend all three appeals honestly, and explain **how** each one moves the listener.

chapters.title: Structuring a speech that holds a room

lines.cap: **Logos:** Every winning speech follows one skeleton: **Happy Speakers Thrill Crowds** — **Hook, Signpost, Three points, Close**!
**Pathos:** First twenty seconds: the **hook**! Open with a **rhetorical question**, a startling **statistic**, a bold claim, or a short **anecdote**.
**Mei:** Put your hand up if a warm, crispy curry puff has ever saved your Tuesday. Keep it up if a rice cake tastes like cardboard!
**Logos:** Better! Step two: **signposting** — a roadmap for listeners who can't flip back a page. 'I have three reasons: heritage, price, and joy.'
**Nib:** Step three: **three points** — the **rule of three**, or **tricolon**, guided by **discourse markers** like 'Firstly' and 'Finally'.
**Ethos:** And include a **counter-argument** and **rebuttal**! Raise their objection — 'Some say fried pastry is unhealthy' — then answer it fairly.
**Mr H:** Step four: the **close**. Give a specific **call to action** using **imperatives**: 'Sign the petition. Vote tomorrow.'
**Nib:** Then **circle back** to your opening hook — a **cyclical structure** — and land one memorable line before 'Thank you'.
**Mei:** Bye-bye 'Hello my name is'. Speech rating: **two and a half stars**!
**Narrator:** Lunchtime. Library. Nib is drilling persuasive devices.
**Nib:** Start with **DAFOREST**: **D**irect address, **A**necdote, **F**acts, **O**pinions, **R**hetorical questions, **E**motive language, **S**tatistics, **T**riplets.
**Pathos:** Now level up! **Anaphora** repeats words at the **start** of clauses — like Martin Luther King's 'I have a dream' or Greta Thunberg's 'How dare you'!
**Nib:** **Epistrophe** repeats at the **end**; **antithesis** balances opposites side by side; **hypophora** asks a question and immediately answers it!
**Mei:** So if I say a mountain of rice cakes taller than the Marina Bay Sands, that's **hyperbole** — deliberate exaggeration?
**Nib:** Precisely, darling! Never just name a device: write **Device + Quotation + Effect on the listener**.
**Logos:** Need proof that shorter beats longer? **Gettysburg, 1863**. The main speaker talked for **two hours**. **Abraham Lincoln** spoke for **two minutes** — about 270 words!
**Mr H:** Lincoln moves cleanly from **past** ('Four score and seven years ago') to **present** war to **future** freedom.
**Ethos:** Listen to his **antithesis**: 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.'
**Nib:** And his closing **tricolon** with **epistrophe**: 'government **of the people, by the people, for the people**'.
**Will:** Enough modern amateurs! To Rome — **Julius Caesar**, Act 3 Scene 2! Brutus has killed Caesar and calmed the crowd in **prose**.
**Logos:** Brutus uses clean **antithesis** and logos: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more.' Then he leaves!
**Will:** Fatal mistake! **Mark Antony** steps up in **blank verse**: '**Friends, Romans, countrymen**, lend me your ears; I come to **bury** Caesar, not to **praise** him.'
**Nib:** Antony promised not to blame Brutus, so he uses **verbal irony** — repeating 'For Brutus is an **honourable** man' beside proof that Caesar cared for Rome!
**Pathos:** Caesar wept for the poor! Refused the crown thrice! By the fifth '**honourable**', praise has curdled into pure **sarcasm**!
**Will:** Then Antony weeps: 'My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar, / And I must pause till it come back to me' — letting the crowd persuade itself!
**Will:** Compare two battle rallies! My **Henry V** uses urgent **imperatives** and animal imagery: 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more' and 'Stiffen the sinews'!
**Ethos:** While **Elizabeth I** at **Tilbury** in **1588** uses a bold concession and **antithesis**: 'I have the body but of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king'!
**Mr H:** On the exam, climb **PEEL**: **Point** — Antony turns the crowd using repetition that becomes **verbal irony**.
**Mei:** **Evidence** & **Explain**: placing '**honourable**' beside 'Caesar hath wept' makes the word sound hollow without breaking his promise.
**Mei:** **Link**: Shakespeare shows rhetoric's dangerous power to steer a crowd while letting them think they chose it themselves!
**Narrator:** Period 5. Final rehearsal in the hall.
**Mr H:** Delivery is half the battle. Change which word you **stress** in 'I never said she stole my money' and you get **seven** different meanings.
**Ethos:** Master the **four Ps** of voice! **Pace**: around 130 to 150 words per minute — about **420 words** for three minutes. Over time? **Cut** lines, don't rush!
**Pathos:** **Projection**: breathe from your diaphragm to the back wall without shouting! **Pitch**: vary intonation — no flat **monotone** and no rising **uptalk**!
**Kevin:** And the best P: **Pause**! Even Mark Antony paused mid-speech! Stop **before** your key line for suspense, and **after** so it sinks in!
**Mei:** Two hundred curry puffs... gone.
**Kevin:** She paused! Two whole seconds! Nobody spliced me! Best day of my life!
**Mr H:** Body: sweep **eye contact** like a lighthouse, use open **gestures**, stand **grounded**, and hold small **keyword cue cards**, never a full script.
**Logos:** Heart pounding? That's adrenaline! Breathe **four in, six out**, relabel 'scared' as '**excited**', and remember the **illusion of transparency**: you look calmer than you feel!
**Mei:** Judges check content, structure, delivery, engagement, and timing. Ready! **Four stars**!
**Narrator:** Before Mei takes the microphone: six public-speaking traps.
**Mei:** Hooks! **GAP**; **Ethos, Pathos, Logos, Kairos**; **Happy Speakers Thrill Crowds**; **DAFOREST**; and the **four Ps**: Pace, Pause, Projection, Pitch!
**Pathos:** One. Never waste your opening on 'Hello, my name is...'. Start with a **hook**!
**Nib:** Two. Don't feature-spot! Use **Device + Quotation + Effect on the listener**.
**Logos:** Three. Don't mix up the appeals: **ethos** is trust, **pathos** is emotion, **logos** is logic and evidence.
**Will:** Four. '**Friends, Romans, countrymen**' is spoken by **Mark Antony**, not Julius Caesar — Caesar is in the coffin!
**Mr H:** Five. Don't write an essay and call it a speech: use **signposting**, **direct address**, and a **call to action**.
**Kevin:** Six. Use **keyword cue cards**, pause around key lines, and never rush over the time limit!
**Narrator:** 4:15 p.m. The canteen keeps the curry puffs.
**Mei:** Public speaking: **four and a half stars**. Deducting half because Will tried to speak for two hours like Edward Everett.
**Will:** Hamlet is four hours, and every syllable is gold!
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Which of Aristotle's appeals relies on the speaker's **credibility and character**?
**Ethos:** **Ethos** — why the audience should trust *you*!
**Mr H:** Repeating a phrase at the **start** of successive clauses is called what?
**Nib:** **Anaphora** — whereas **epistrophe** repeats at the end.
**Mr H:** Who says '**Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears**', and in which play?
**Will:** **Mark Antony**, in **Julius Caesar**, Act 3 Scene 2!
**Mr H:** Why does Mark Antony keep calling Brutus '**an honourable man**'?
**Mei:** **Verbal irony**! Placed beside evidence of Caesar's goodness, it sounds more sarcastic each time without breaking his promise.
**Mr H:** What are the **four Ps** of vocal delivery?
**Kevin:** **Pace, Pause, Projection, and Pitch**! Especially Pause!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Public Speaking & Rhetoric** quiz in your English Lab.
**Kevin:** Wait... everybody hold a dramatic pause...
**Kevin:** Nailed it.
